nameStory: Sorastrum gets its name from the Greek words 'soros' meaning heap and 'astron' meaning star, perfectly describing how these tiny algae arrange themselves in star-like clusters. The species name 'spinulosum' means 'with little spines,' referring to the delicate spiny projections that extend from each cell like microscopic sea urchins.
description: Sorastrum spinulosum is a microscopic freshwater green algae that forms beautiful star-shaped colonies visible only under magnification. Each colony consists of 4-32 individual cells arranged in a flat, circular pattern, with each cell sporting delicate spines that radiate outward. The entire colony is typically smaller than the width of a human hair, measuring just 20-100 micrometers across. While invisible to the naked eye, these tiny organisms can sometimes give pond water a faint greenish tinge when present in large numbers.

idTips.label: Star-shaped colony arrangement
idTips.description: Cells are arranged in a perfect flat, circular pattern like spokes on a wheel or points on a star, never in chains or irregular clusters

idTips.label: Spiny cell projections
idTips.description: Each cell has 1-4 delicate, needle-like spines extending outward that are clearly visible under microscope magnification

idTips.label: Colony size
idTips.description: Entire star-shaped colony measures 20-100 micrometers across, requiring at least 100x magnification to see clearly

idTips.label: Bright green coloration
idTips.description: Cells appear bright emerald green under the microscope due to their chloroplasts, never blue-green or brownish

idTips.label: Flat colony structure
idTips.description: All cells lie in the same plane creating a flat, disc-like appearance rather than a three-dimensional sphere

habitat: Found floating freely in the plankton of quiet freshwater ponds, small lakes, and slow-moving streams throughout New England. Prefers nutrient-rich waters with neutral to slightly alkaline pH, often in areas with some organic matter. Most commonly discovered in shallow, sun-warmed waters during warmer months where other microscopic life is abundant.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to grow as water temperatures rise above 50°F, though still relatively uncommon in early spring samples.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance occurs during warm summer months when water temperatures are highest and nutrients are most available for growth.
seasonality.fall: Numbers decline as temperatures drop, but colonies may still be found in protected areas with warmer water temperatures.
seasonality.winter: Largely absent from water samples as the species cannot tolerate freezing temperatures and goes dormant.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, a single drop of pond water can contain hundreds of these microscopic 'stars,' and each perfect star-shaped colony reproduces by having its cells simultaneously release tiny swimming spores that eventually settle down to form new star colonies elsewhere.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other star-shaped microscopic algae like Pediastrum, but Sorastrum's spiny projections and smaller colony size help distinguish it - remember 'Sorastrum has Spines' as a memory trick.
contextualKnowledge: This is a planktonic algae that requires microscopic examination to identify, so it's primarily of interest to pond study enthusiasts, students with microscopes, or citizen scientists participating in freshwater monitoring programs rather than casual nature observers.
compareHints: Sorastrum spinulosum differs from its relative Sorastrum americanum primarily in spine arrangement and colony structure - S. spinulosum has more prominent spines and typically forms flatter, more regular star patterns. Both species are much smaller and more delicately spined than the related but larger Pediastrum species in the same family.
